claim: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are membrane proteins which activate cellular signaling in response to extracellular stimuli.
source: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are membrane proteins which activate cellular signaling in response to extracellular stimuli.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about GPCR function.

claim: GPCRs are vital in many physiological processes and constitute the most common class of drug targets.
source: GPCRs are vital in many physiological processes and constitute the most common class of drug targets (Hauser et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hauser et al., 2017.

claim: The β2 adrenergic receptor was the first receptor crystallized in complex with a G protein.
source: The β2AR is a drug target for bronchoconstriction medication and was the first receptor crystallized in complex with a G protein (Rasmussen et al., 2011a; Rasmussen et al., 2011b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rasmussen et al., 2011a and 2011b.

claim: GPCRs interconvert between inactive (R) and active (R*) states, which control G protein binding to a conserved intracellular domain via conformational rearrangements among the seven transmembrane (TM) helices.
source: GPCRs interconvert between inactive (R) and active (R*) states, which control G protein binding to a conserved intracellular domain via conformational rearrangements among the seven transmembrane (TM) helices (Figure 1a; Manglik and Kruse, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Manglik and Kruse, 2017 and reference to Figure 1a.

claim: Agonists bound in experimental structures show a key interaction with S207(5.46).
source: Agonists bound in experimental structures show a key interaction with S207(5.46) (Chan et al., 2016) and an inward bulge of TM5 in the active state.
evidence: Supported by citation to Chan et al., 2016.

claim: After 305 iterations, corresponding to 4 µs of aggregated simulation time per ligand-receptor complex, the activation pathways had converged.
source: After 305 iterations, corresponding to 4 µs of aggregated simulation time per ligand-receptor complex, the activation pathways had converged (Table 1 and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–6).
evidence: Supported by reference to Table 1 and Figure 2 supplements showing convergence data.

claim: The expectation values associated with the TM5 bulge microswitch were strongly correlated to experimentally reported cAMP production (R = −0.95).
source: Remarkably, the expectation values associated with the upper microswitches were strongly correlated to the previously reported experimental values, in particular the TM5 bulge (Figure 2c; R = −0.95) and the connector ΔRMSD (Figure 2d; R = 0.93).
evidence: Supported by correlation coefficient and reference to Figure 2c showing the correlation.

claim: The expectation values associated with the connector ΔRMSD microswitch were strongly correlated to experimentally reported cAMP production (R = 0.93).
source: Remarkably, the expectation values associated with the upper microswitches were strongly correlated to the previously reported experimental values, in particular the TM5 bulge (Figure 2c; R = −0.95) and the connector ΔRMSD (Figure 2d; R = 0.93).
evidence: Supported by correlation coefficient and reference to Figure 2d showing the correlation.

claim: BI-167107 is predicted to have a cAMP Emax value slightly higher than adrenaline and salmeterol.
source: we predicted BI-167107 to have a cAMP Emax value slightly higher than adrenaline and salmeterol, and carazolol to have an Emax similar to the values of the ligand free receptor and inverse agonist timolol (Figure 2c,d).
evidence: Predicted from linear regression based on simulation data, shown in Figure 2c,d.

claim: Carazolol is predicted to have an Emax similar to the values of the ligand free receptor and inverse agonist timolol.
source: we predicted BI-167107 to have a cAMP Emax value slightly higher than adrenaline and salmeterol, and carazolol to have an Emax similar to the values of the ligand free receptor and inverse agonist timolol (Figure 2c,d).
evidence: Predicted from linear regression based on simulation data, shown in Figure 2c,d.

claim: BI-167107 is a known full agonist.
source: These results are in line with expectations; BI-167107 is indeed a known full agonist and carazolol an inverse agonist (Manglik et al., 2015; Rasmussen et al., 2011a; Ueda et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Manglik et al., 2015; Rasmussen et al., 2011a; Ueda et al., 2019.

claim: Carazolol is an inverse agonist.
source: These results are in line with expectations; BI-167107 is indeed a known full agonist and carazolol an inverse agonist (Manglik et al., 2015; Rasmussen et al., 2011a; Ueda et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Manglik et al., 2015; Rasmussen et al., 2011a; Ueda et al., 2019.

claim: The cAMP response was less well correlated with the expectation values of the Y-Y motif (R = −0.75).
source: Moving down the microswitch cascade toward the intracellular region, the cAMP response was less well correlated with the expectation values and the ΔG of the Y-Y motif and Ionic lock distance (Figure 2e; R = −0.75 and Figure 2f; R = 0.58, respectively, and Figure 2—figure supplement 8), as expected from the looser coupling between these microswitches and the ligand binding sites.
evidence: Supported by correlation coefficient and reference to Figure 2e.

claim: The cAMP response was less well correlated with the expectation values of the Ionic lock distance (R = 0.58).
source: Moving down the microswitch cascade toward the intracellular region, the cAMP response was less well correlated with the expectation values and the ΔG of the Y-Y motif and Ionic lock distance (Figure 2e; R = −0.75 and Figure 2f; R = 0.58, respectively, and Figure 2—figure supplement 8), as expected from the looser coupling between these microswitches and the ligand binding sites.
evidence: Supported by correlation coefficient and reference to Figure 2f.

claim: 19F-fluorine NMR and double electron-electron resonance (DEER) spectroscopy experiments have shown that the conformational ensembles of carazolol and the apo receptor have similar TM6 distance distributions.
source: 19F-fluorine NMR and double electron-electron resonance (DEER) spectroscopy experiments have shown that the conformational ensembles of carazolol and the apo receptor have similar TM6 distance distributions (Manglik et al., 2015), in agreement with the similarity in their microswitch expectation values and free energy landscapes (Figure 2b,f and Figure 2—figure supplement 8e).
evidence: Supported by citation to Manglik et al., 2015.

claim: The simulation results showing similar TM6 distance distributions for carazolol and apo receptor are in agreement with spectroscopy experiments.
source: 19F-fluorine NMR and double electron-electron resonance (DEER) spectroscopy experiments have shown that the conformational ensembles of carazolol and the apo receptor have similar TM6 distance distributions (Manglik et al., 2015), in agreement with the similarity in their microswitch expectation values and free energy landscapes (Figure 2b,f and Figure 2—figure supplement 8e).
evidence: Comparison between simulation data (Figure 2b,f) and experimental data from Manglik et al., 2015.

claim: The inactive receptor exists in two sub-states, one with a formed and one with a broken ionic lock.
source: It has also been proposed that the inactive receptor exists in two sub-states (Manglik et al., 2015), one with a formed and one with a broken ionic lock.
evidence: Supported by citation to Manglik et al., 2015.

claim: The simulations rarely captured a sub-state with the ionic lock formed, suggesting that the state with a broken ionic lock is of lower free energy.
source: Our simulations rarely captured a sub-state with the ionic lock formed, which suggest that the state with a broken ionic lock is of lower free energy, although modeling of missing residues in the cytosolic domain of TM6 and TM3 may alter the dynamics of this region (Dror et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on simulation observations and inference about free energy, with caveat about modeling limitations.

claim: Agonists stabilized a state with the side chains of the ionic lock residues pointing away from each other.
source: Nevertheless, the agonists stabilized a state with the side chains of the ionic lock residues pointing away from each other, while the inverse agonist carazolol favored a state with the side chains pointing toward each other, although the TM6 displacement was too large for the residues to fully form an ionic bond (Figure 2—figure supplement 11a).
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 11a.

claim: The inverse agonist carazolol favored a state with the ionic lock side chains pointing toward each other.
source: Nevertheless, the agonists stabilized a state with the side chains of the ionic lock residues pointing away from each other, while the inverse agonist carazolol favored a state with the side chains pointing toward each other, although the TM6 displacement was too large for the residues to fully form an ionic bond (Figure 2—figure supplement 11a).
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 11a.

claim: β2AR crystal structures reveal a number of stabilized water molecules in the inactive state, while this region is dehydrated in the G protein-bound state.
source: β2AR crystal structures reveal a number of stabilized water molecules in the inactive state, while this region is dehydrated in the G protein-bound state (Cherezov et al., 2007; Rasmussen et al., 2011b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cherezov et al., 2007 and Rasmussen et al., 2011b.

claim: The disruption of intra-receptor water networks and the formation of a hydrophobic barrier are likely conserved features of activation.
source: The disruption of intra-receptor water networks and the formation of a hydrophobic barrier, a prerequisite of activation (Trzaskowski et al. 2012), are likely conserved features of activation (Venkatakrishnan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Trzaskowski et al. 2012 and Venkatakrishnan et al., 2019.

claim: BI-167107 stabilized a partially dehydrated active state when TM6 assumed its outward pose.
source: We investigated the hydration near the intracellular binding site by counting the number of water molecules within 0.8 nm of L266(6.28) (Figure 2—figure supplement 11b), and found that BI-167107 stabilized a partially dehydrated active state when TM6 assumed its outward pose.
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 11b.

claim: Carazolol and the apo condition did not induce dehydration with TM6 in its active conformation.
source: Carazolol and the apo condition, on the other hand, did not induce dehydration with TM6 in its active conformation (Figure 2—figure supplement 11b).
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 11b.

claim: Ligands share many overall features of activation, but stabilize unique local states.
source: To summarize, an analysis of the simulations by machine learning shows that ligands share many overall features of activation, but stabilize unique local states, in agreement with previous work (Kohlhoff et al., 2014; Tikhonova et al., 2013; Provasi et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2012; Lamichhane et al., 2020; Frei et al., 2020; Suomivuori et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by machine learning analysis of simulation data and citations to previous work.

claim: The NPxxY motif and the intracellular part of TM6 were identified as the most important regions for classification of ligand-bound states.
source: Remarkably, both data-driven methods identified established microswitches as the most important regions for classification: the NPxxY motif and the intracellular part of TM6 in the intracellular binding site (Figure 4a,b and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data-driven analysis shown in Figure 4a,b and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The TM5 bulge was particularly important for discriminating between agonists and non-agonists.
source: The TM5 bulge was particularly important for discriminating between agonists and non-agonists (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by data-driven analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The NPxxY motif assumed a unique conformation for each ligand.
source: The NPxxY motif, on the other hand, assumed a unique conformation for each ligand (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by data-driven analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Spectroscopy experiments have shown that the agonist BI-167107 stabilizes an intermediate, pre-active state.
source: Spectroscopy experiments have shown that the agonist BI-167107 stabilizes an intermediate, pre-active state (Manglik et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Manglik et al., 2015.

claim: Receptor activation involves a transition via a pre-active state before forming the fully active state together with an intracellular binding partner.
source: It was hypothesized that receptor activation involves a transition via this state before forming the fully active state together with an intracellular binding partner (Manglik et al., 2015).
evidence: Hypothesis from Manglik et al., 2015.

claim: Different agonists induced different states in the cytoplasmic domain according to spectroscopy experiments.
source: Moreover, spectroscopy experiments found that different agonists induced different states in the cytoplasmic domain (Manglik et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Manglik et al., 2015.

claim: The region around the NPxxY domain is a major source of conformational heterogeneity.
source: Our results provide molecular models for the pre-active ensemble, and identified the region around the NPxxY domain a major source of conformational heterogeneity (Figure 4b and Figure 4—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figure 4b and Figure 4—figure supplements 1–4.

claim: Conformational differences in the NPxxY domain have been shown to correlate to efficacy and biased signaling in spectroscopy experiments.
source: In agreement, conformational differences in this domain have been shown to correlate to efficacy and biased signaling in 19F NMR and single-molecule fluorescence spectroscopy experiments (Frei et al., 2020; Lamichhane et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Frei et al., 2020; Lamichhane et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2012.

claim: Agonists exercise direct control of TM5, where agonists and non-agonists stabilize different states.
source: Ligands exercise direct control of TM5, where agonists and non-agonists stabilize different states.
evidence: Based on analysis of simulation data and conceptual model in Figure 4d.

claim: Residues approximately one helical turn below the orthosteric site, including the connector region, couple to the conformations in the orthosteric site.
source: In turn, residues approximately one helical turn below the orthosteric site—including the connector region, which was identified as a good predictor of downstream response (Figure 2d)—couple to the conformations in the orthosteric site.
evidence: Based on analysis of simulation data and reference to Figure 2d.

claim: V206(5.46) could form van der Waals interactions with T118(3.37) only in the presence of agonists.
source: We found that V206(5.46) could form van der Waals interactions with T118(3.37) only in the presence of agonists (Figure 5a and b).
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figure 5a and b.

claim: Agonists induce a contraction between L284(6.46) and F321(7.48) in the TM domain compared to non-agonists.
source: In the TM domain, agonists induce a contraction between L284(6.46) and F321(7.48) (Figure 5a and b) compared to non-agonists.
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figure 5a and b.

claim: The backbone carbonyl of S319(7.46) formed a hydrogen bond with the side chain of N51(1.50) on TM1 for agonists, whereas this interaction was destabilized for the other ligands.
source: In this region, our machine-learning analysis also identified that the backbone carbonyl of S319(7.46) formed a hydrogen bond with the side chain of N51(1.50) on TM1 for agonists, whereas this interaction was destabilized for the other ligands (Figure 5d).
evidence: Supported by machine learning analysis and simulation data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: N51(1.50) is one of the most conserved residues across class A GPCRs.
source: N51(1.50) is one of the most conserved residues across class A GPCRs (Isberg et al., 2014) and stabilizes a water network together with D79(2.50) and Y326(7.53) in the inactive receptor (Cherezov et al., 2007; Venkatakrishnan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Isberg et al., 2014; Cherezov et al., 2007; Venkatakrishnan et al., 2019.

claim: N51(1.50) stabilizes a water network together with D79(2.50) and Y326(7.53) in the inactive receptor.
source: N51(1.50) is one of the most conserved residues across class A GPCRs (Isberg et al., 2014) and stabilizes a water network together with D79(2.50) and Y326(7.53) in the inactive receptor (Cherezov et al., 2007; Venkatakrishnan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cherezov et al., 2007; Venkatakrishnan et al., 2019.

claim: Agonists favored contractions between local inter-residue distances compared to non-agonists.
source: Overall, agonists favored contractions between local inter-residue distances compared to non-agonists.
evidence: Based on analysis of simulation data.

claim: Agonist-bound receptors showed a contraction of the entire protein, as reflected by the decrease in distance between S203(5.43) and E338(8.56) on helix 8 (H8) and between S207(5.46) and V307(7.33) across the orthosteric binding site.
source: By inspecting the most substantially changing large-scale distances, we also identified a contraction of the entire protein for agonist-bound receptors, as reflected by the decrease in distance between S203(5.43) and E338(8.56) on helix 8 (H8) and between S207(5.46) and V307(7.33) across the orthosteric binding site (Figure 5a and c).
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figure 5a and c.

claim: Adrenaline favored the most active-like NPxxY motif, with Y326(7.53) closer to L275(6.37).
source: Adrenaline favored the most active-like NPxxY motif, which was also maintained throughout its activation path (Fig. S7d), with Y326(7.53) closer to L275(6.37) (Figure 5d).
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Salmeterol stabilized a distinct NPxxY conformation in which Y326(7.53) underwent a rotation, bringing the tyrosine's side chain further into the interface between TM6 and TM7.
source: Salmeterol stabilized a distinct NPxxY conformation, which was also observed in the activation path ensemble (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), in which Y326(7.53) underwent a rotation, bringing the tyrosine's side chain further into the interface between TM6 and TM7.
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The NPxxY conformation stabilized by salmeterol is reminiscent of conformations suggested by 19F NMR studies on the β1-adrenergic receptor.
source: This pose is reminiscent of conformations suggested by 19F NMR studies on the β1-adrenergic receptor (Frei et al., 2020).
evidence: Comparison to experimental data from Frei et al., 2020.

claim: BI-167107 stabilized an inactive-like NPxxY motif with Y326(7.53) pointing away from L275(6.37).
source: BI-167107 stabilized an inactive-like NPxxY motif with Y326(7.53) pointing away from L275(6.37) (Figure 5d).
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The data-driven approach automatically identified highly conserved residues involved in receptor activation.
source: In general, our data-driven approach automatically identified highly conserved residues involved in receptor activation (Figure 4).
evidence: Based on machine learning analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: V206(5.46) and S207(5.46) were shown to interact with a recently discovered negative allosteric modulator that binds in an extrahelical site adjacent to the PIF motif.
source: V206(5.46) and S207(5.46) were shown to interact with a recently discovered negative allosteric modulator that binds in an extrahelical site adjacent to the PIF motif (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2020.

claim: Signaling hotspots near the NPxxY motif experience the largest ligand-induced conformational heterogeneity.
source: Our results do not only illustrate the usefulness of MD combined with data-driven analysis; they allow us to identify potential allosteric sites that can be targeted by ligands, and reveal that, against our expectations, signaling hotspots near the NPxxY motif, far away from the orthosteric site, experience the largest ligand-induced conformational heterogeneity.
evidence: Based on analysis of simulation data.

claim: The β2AR interacts with Gs proteins to trigger a cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) response.
source: In this study, we focus on the prototypical β2 adrenergic receptor (β2AR), which interacts with Gs proteins to trigger a cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) response, and arrestins, which control endocytosis and kinase activation (Jean-Charles et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jean-Charles et al., 2017.

claim: The β2AR interacts with arrestins, which control endocytosis and kinase activation.
source: In this study, we focus on the prototypical β2 adrenergic receptor (β2AR), which interacts with Gs proteins to trigger a cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) response, and arrestins, which control endocytosis and kinase activation (Jean-Charles et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jean-Charles et al., 2017.

claim: The β2AR is a drug target for bronchoconstriction medication.
source: The β2AR is a drug target for bronchoconstriction medication and was the first receptor crystallized in complex with a G protein (Rasmussen et al., 2011a; Rasmussen et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is established knowledge about β2AR therapeutic applications.

claim: The connector region was identified as a good predictor of downstream response.
source: In turn, residues approximately one helical turn below the orthosteric site—including the connector region, which was identified as a good predictor of downstream response (Figure 2d)—couple to the conformations in the orthosteric site.
evidence: Based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 2d.

claim: GPCRs only assume their fully active state in the presence of an intracellular binding partner.
source: GPCRs only assume their fully active state in the presence of an intracellular binding partner (Gregorio et al., 2017; Manglik et al., 2015; Nygaard et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gregorio et al., 2017; Manglik et al., 2015; Nygaard et al., 2013.

claim: The β2AR undergoes basal activity, where it fluctuates between active-like and inactive states.
source: The β2AR undergoes a basal activity, where it fluctuates between active-like and inactive states (Gregorio et al., 2017; Lamichhane et al., 2015), which can be inferred from the relatively low free energy difference between the basins in the energy landscapes.
evidence: Supported by citations to Gregorio et al., 2017; Lamichhane et al., 2015 and inference from simulation data.

claim: Extracellular and TM microswitches only require an agonist to maintain their active state conformations.
source: While extracellular and TM microswitches only require an agonist to maintain their active state conformations, intracellular microswitches interact with an intracellular binding partner directly and are more affected by its absence, which is likely why correlations between microswitch expectation value and Emax are worse for the intracellular microswitches.
evidence: Based on inference from simulation data and understanding of GPCR activation.

claim: Intracellular microswitches interact with an intracellular binding partner directly and are more affected by its absence.
source: While extracellular and TM microswitches only require an agonist to maintain their active state conformations, intracellular microswitches interact with an intracellular binding partner directly and are more affected by its absence, which is likely why correlations between microswitch expectation value and Emax are worse for the intracellular microswitches.
evidence: Based on inference from simulation data and understanding of GPCR activation.

claim: The reorganization of H8 may be a secondary effect due to modulation of the NPxxY motif.
source: While the reorganization of H8 may be a secondary effect due to modulation of the NPxxY motif, this region could be important for arrestin recruitment (Lally et al., 2017; Staus et al., 2018).
evidence: Speculation based on simulation observations and citations to Lally et al., 2017; Staus et al., 2018.

claim: The H8 region could be important for arrestin recruitment.
source: While the reorganization of H8 may be a secondary effect due to modulation of the NPxxY motif, this region could be important for arrestin recruitment (Lally et al., 2017; Staus et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lally et al., 2017; Staus et al., 2018.

claim: Salmeterol's distinct NPxxY state only formed in combination with a lost interaction between salmeterol and S207(5.46) and S203(5.43).
source: Salmeterol's distinct NPxxY state only formed in combination with a lost interaction between salmeterol and S207(5.46) and S203(5.43), which is remarkable considering that the two binding sites are believed to be only loosely coupled (Dror et al., 2011; Fleetwood et al., 2020b).
evidence: Based on simulation data and comparison to previous work (Dror et al., 2011; Fleetwood et al., 2020b).

claim: A similar phenomenon to salmeterol's lost interaction with S207(5.46) and S203(5.43) has been reported in a recent structure of β1AR, where the corresponding serines experienced weakened interactions to the biased agonist formoterol.
source: A similar phenomenon has been reported in a recent structure of β1AR (Lee et al., 2020), where the corresponding serines in the orthosteric site experienced weakened interactions to the biased agonist formoterol.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2020.

claim: Y(7.53) forms contacts with arrestin for β1AR.
source: The fact that Y(7.53) forms contacts with arrestin for β1AR (Lee et al., 2020) suggests that our derived β2AR conformation may have biased signaling properties.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2020.

claim: The derived β2AR conformation may have biased signaling properties.
source: The fact that Y(7.53) forms contacts with arrestin for β1AR (Lee et al., 2020) suggests that our derived β2AR conformation may have biased signaling properties.
evidence: Speculation based on comparison to β1AR data from Lee et al., 2020.

claim: The activation pathways as well as the stabilized states are significantly altered upon ligand binding.
source: Our results show that the activation pathways as well as the stabilized states are significantly altered upon ligand binding, and that ligands with shared efficacy profiles generate similar, albeit not identical, ensembles of states.
evidence: Based on analysis of simulation data.

claim: Ligands with shared efficacy profiles generate similar, albeit not identical, ensembles of states.
source: Our results show that the activation pathways as well as the stabilized states are significantly altered upon ligand binding, and that ligands with shared efficacy profiles generate similar, albeit not identical, ensembles of states.
evidence: Based on analysis of simulation data.

claim: Two ligands which lead to a similar downstream response do not necessarily stabilize the same receptor conformations.
source: It therefore cannot be taken for granted that two ligands which lead to a similar downstream response necessarily stabilize the same receptor conformations.
evidence: Based on inference from simulation data showing conformational heterogeneity.

claim: The simulations used the CHARMM36m force field.
source: We initiated simulation systems from a nanobody-bound active-state BI-167017-bound structure (PDB ID: 3P0G) (Rasmussen et al., 2011a) and an inactive carazolol-bound structure (PDB ID: 2RH1) (Cherezov et al., 2007) in CHARMM-GUI (Lee et al., 2016) with the CHARMM36m force field (Huang et al., 2017).
evidence: Explicit description of simulation methodology.

claim: The receptor was embedded in a POPC membrane bilayer of 180 molecules.
source: The receptor was embedded in a POPC membrane bilayer (Klauda et al., 2010) of 180 molecules, then solvated in a 0.15M concentration of neutralizing sodium and chloride ions with 79 TIP3P water molecules (Jorgensen et al., 1983) per lipid molecule.
evidence: Explicit description of simulation system setup.

claim: MD simulations were performed with GROMACS 2018.6 patched with PLUMED.
source: We performed the MD simulations with GROMACS 2018.6 (Abraham et al., 2015) patched with PLUMED (Tribello et al., 2014).
evidence: Explicit description of simulation software.

claim: The string method with swarms of trajectories finds the most probable transition pathway between two end states in a high-dimensional space spanned by a set of CVs.
source: This method finds the most probable transition pathway between two end states in a high-dimensional space spanned by a set of CVs (in this context synonymous with reaction coordinates).
evidence: Description of the computational method used.

claim: Convergence is generally reached when the string diffuses around an equilibrium position.
source: Convergence is generally reached when the string diffuses around an equilibrium position.
evidence: Description of convergence criterion for the method.

claim: The average strings for all ligand–receptor complexes had converged after 305 iterations.
source: To evaluate the convergence we averaged the strings over 60 iterations, and stopped sampling every simulation after 305 iterations, at which point the average strings for all ligand–receptor complexes had converged.
evidence: Based on convergence analysis of simulation data.

claim: The CVs for the string method were derived in a data-driven manner from the swarm coordinates of the apo simulation's final iteration using demystifying software.
source: We derived the CVs for the string method with swarms of trajectories in a data-driven manner from the swarm coordinates of the apo simulation's final iteration using demystifying (Fleetwood et al., 2020c), a software which utilizes machine learning tools and dimensionality reduction methods to identify important features from MD simulation trajectories.
evidence: Description of methodology for CV selection.

claim: A restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) was used to identify important features for collective variables.
source: We then used the features to train a restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) (Smolensky, 1986). An RBM is a single-layer neural network with a number of hidden components (two in this manuscript), equivalent to a fully connected bipartite graph.
evidence: Description of machine learning methodology.

claim: Free energy landscapes were estimated by discretizing a grid along chosen variables and constructing a regularized transition matrix from the swarm trajectories' transitions between bins.
source: Free energy landscapes were estimated during post-processing by discretizing a grid along a chosen set of variables and constructing a regularized transition matrix from the swarm trajectories' transitions between bins.
evidence: Description of free energy estimation methodology.

claim: A Bayesian Markov chain Monte Carlo method was applied to sample 1000 different transition matrices from the dataset to estimate convergence of the free energy landscapes.
source: To estimate the convergence of the free energy landscapes, we applied a Bayesian Markov chain Monte Carlo method (Harrigan et al., 2017) to sample 1000 different transition matrices from the dataset, each with a corresponding probability distribution and free energy landscape.
evidence: Description of statistical analysis methodology.

claim: Principal component analysis (PCA) seeks a linear transformation of the input data into an orthogonal basis of principal components.
source: PCA seeks a linear transformation of the input data into an orthogonal basis of principal components (PCs) and is designed to cover as much of the variance in the data as possible (Figure 3a).
evidence: Description of PCA methodology.

claim: Multidimensional scaling (MDS) projects the high dimensional space into a low dimensional representation using a non-linear transformation which preserves the distance between points.
source: MDS projects the high dimensional space into a low dimensional representation using a non-linear transformation which preserves the distance between points (Figure 3b).
evidence: Description of MDS methodology.

claim: T-SNE is a visualization technique which seeks to disentangle a high-dimensional data set by transforming it into a low-dimensional embedding where similar points are near each other and dissimilar objects have a high probability of being distant.
source: T-SNE is a visualization technique which seeks to disentangle a high-dimensional data set by transforming it into a low-dimensional embedding where similar points are near each other and dissimilar objects have a high probability of being distant (Figure 3c).
evidence: Description of t-SNE methodology.

claim: The dimensionality reduction techniques created embeddings which separated snapshots by their progression along the activation path for the converged activation pathways.
source: For the latter, which represent the converged activation pathways, the dimensionality reduction techniques created embeddings which separated snapshots by their progression along the activation path (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on dimensionality reduction analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Unsupervised dimensionality reduction methods tend to emphasize large scale amplitude motions, such as the displacement of TM6 in the case of GPCR activation.
source: This is expected because unsupervised dimensionality reduction methods tend to emphasize large scale amplitude motions, such as the displacement of TM6 in the case of GPCR activation (Fleetwood et al., 2020c).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fleetwood et al., 2020c.

claim: After eight iterations with an accumulated simulation time of 1.4 μs per ligand, the method for finding single equilibrated states generated trajectories that diffused around the most stabilized state kinetically accessible from the starting structure.
source: Indeed, after eight iterations with an accumulated simulation time of 1.4 μs per ligand (see Materials and methods), the method for finding single equilibrated states generated trajectories that diffused around the most stabilized state kinetically accessible from the starting structure (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on adaptive sampling analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dividing the dataset into thirds yielded similar results, showing that the states were adequately sampled.
source: Dividing the dataset into thirds yielded similar results (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), showing that the states were adequately sampled.
evidence: Based on cross-validation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The details of the active state ensemble varied among the ligands.
source: The details of the active state ensemble varied among the ligands (Figure 3a–c).
evidence: Based on dimensionality reduction analysis shown in Figure 3a–c.

claim: Simulations with agonists bound tended to be grouped together for all three dimensionality reduction methods.
source: Simulations with agonists bound tended to be grouped together for all three dimensionality reduction methods, but each of them generally also led to a distinct conformational ensemble.
evidence: Based on dimensionality reduction analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The simulation snapshots with the agonist adrenaline bound were generally close to the full agonist BI-167107 and the partial agonist salmeterol.
source: The simulation snapshots with the agonist adrenaline bound were generally close to the full agonist BI-167107 and the partial agonist salmeterol.
evidence: Based on dimensionality reduction analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The similarity matrix based on the average distance between snapshots in the full feature space showed that agonists and non-agonists stabilized significantly different states.
source: In agreement with the projections, the similarity matrix based on the average distance between snapshots in the full feature space (Figure 3d) showed that agonists and non-agonists stabilized significantly different states.
evidence: Based on similarity analysis shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The first two principal components are not sufficient to completely separate the dataset according to the ligands present.
source: Using PCA, we note that timolol clusters together with the agonist ligands. Thus, the first two PCs are not sufficient to completely separate the dataset according to the ligands present (Figure 3a), but including more PCs in the projection leads to a satisfactory separation (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Based on PCA analysis shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The non-linear dimensionality reduction methods separated the ligand classes well in two dimensions.
source: The non-linear methods separated the classes well in two dimensions.
evidence: Based on MDS and t-SNE analysis shown in Figure 3b,c.

claim: Although t-SNE generates an embedding with perfect separation between classes, the micro-clusters depend on parametrization of the method and their exact placement is stochastic.
source: We also note that although t-SNE generates an embedding with perfect separation between classes, the micro-clusters depend on parametrization of the method and their exact placement is stochastic (Schubert, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schubert, 2017 and understanding of t-SNE methodology.

claim: PCA analysis of the swarms of trajectories datasets identified parts of TM6 and TM7 near the G protein-binding site as particularly important.
source: To capture the important characteristics of receptor activation, we applied PCA on the swarms of trajectories datasets representing the activation ensemble and extracted important features from these (Figure 4c). This analysis identified parts of TM6 and TM7 near the G protein-binding site as particularly important (Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), adding further support for the importance of these microswitches for activation.
evidence: Based on PCA analysis shown in Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Importance profiles were computed for discriminating between agonists and non-agonists using a symmetrized version of the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence.
source: Importance profiles were computed for discriminating between agonists and non-agonists (Figure 4a) and to distinguish all ligands from each other (Figure 4b) using a symmetrized version of the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence (Fleetwood et al., 2020c; Kullback and Leibler, 1951).
evidence: Description of methodology and reference to Figure 4a,b.

claim: A random forest (RF) classifier was used as a control to evaluate important features.
source: As a control, we also evaluated the important features learned by a random forest (RF) classifier, a machine learning classifier constructed by an ensemble of decision trees.
evidence: Description of control methodology.

claim: The importance profiles of the KL and RF feature extractors were similar.
source: The importance profiles of the KL and RF feature extractors were similar, although the RF classifier generated importance profiles with more distinct peaks.
evidence: Based on comparison of feature importance methods shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The RF classifier probably suppressed some features to enhance prediction accuracy for frames that fluctuated outside the equilibrated states.
source: Since the datasets included a few simulation frames that fluctuated outside the equilibrated states, the RF classifier probably suppressed some features to enhance prediction accuracy for these frames.
evidence: Inference about RF classifier behavior based on understanding of the method.

claim: KL divergence estimated how much the distributions overlapped along individual features and was therefore less likely to discard features based on outlier frames.
source: KL divergence estimated how much the distributions overlapped along individual features and was therefore less likely to discard features based on these frames.
evidence: Explanation of KL divergence methodology.

claim: Differences in the NPxxY motif and intracellular part of TM6 are related to biased signaling.
source: These results underpin experimental evidence that differences in these regions are related to biased signaling (Frei et al., 2020; Lamichhane et al., 2020, Lamichhane et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2012; Suomivuori et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Frei et al., 2020; Lamichhane et al., 2020, Lamichhane et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2012; Suomivuori et al., 2020.

claim: The TM5 conformations within agonists and non-agonists were so similar that this region could not be used to discriminate agonists from each other.
source: This region does not show up as important when differentiating between all ligands (Figure 4b), which means that the TM5 conformations within the two groups of ligands were so similar that this region could not be used to, for example, discriminate agonists from each other.
evidence: Based on feature importance analysis shown in Figure 4b and inference.
